lessonTitle: Global Infectious Disease: Burden, Zoonotic Spillover and Surveillance

blocks.text: In a forest village a hunter dies after butchering a sick animal, a nurse who cared for him falls ill a week later, and by the time a distant laboratory confirms the diagnosis, two further clusters have appeared in neighbouring districts. Whether this becomes a handful of cases or a national epidemic depends less on the virus than on how quickly someone noticed, counted and acted.

blocks.markdown: Infectious diseases remain among the leading causes of death worldwide, with a burden that falls most heavily on low- and middle-income countries. Three infections in particular dominate global health planning: **HIV**, **tuberculosis (TB)** and **malaria**. Global figures change year by year and are estimates, so the numbers below are approximate orders of magnitude; consult current World Health Organization reports for exact values.

blocks.caption: Global burden of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria (approximate, changing annually)
rows: About 40 million people living with HIV; about one million new infections and several hundred thousand deaths yearly
About 10 million new cases yearly; over one million deaths; among the leading infectious causes of death
South-East Asia, Africa and the Western Pacific; many cases in a few high-burden countries
About 250 million cases and over half a million deaths yearly
Sub-Saharan Africa; most deaths in young children

blocks.markdown: These diseases interact. **HIV is the strongest risk factor for progression of latent TB to active TB**, and TB is a leading cause of death among people with HIV; HIV and TB treatment must be coordinated. Malaria and poverty reinforce each other, and malaria in pregnancy harms mother and fetus. Control relies on **prevention** (antiretroviral treatment that also prevents transmission, condoms and pre-exposure prophylaxis; TB case-finding, treatment and BCG vaccine; insecticide-treated bed nets, vector control, malaria vaccines and chemoprevention), **diagnosis**, **effective drug treatment**, and strong health systems, with **drug resistance** an increasing threat to all three.

blocks.title: Reading burden data
blocks.prompt: A country reports 450 new TB cases in a year in a population of 3.0 million. Calculate the incidence per 100 000 and explain why this measure is used rather than raw case numbers.

steps.text: Incidence per 100 000 = cases / population x 100 000 = 450 / 3 000 000 x 100 000.
Rates adjust for population size, so places with different populations can be compared fairly.

blocks.answer: 15 per 100 000 per year; rates allow fair comparison across populations.

blocks.title: Zoonosis and spillover
blocks.text: A zoonosis is an infection transmitted from vertebrate animals to humans. Spillover is the event in which a pathogen from an animal reservoir infects a human. Most spillovers are dead ends, but if the pathogen can transmit efficiently between humans, an outbreak or pandemic can follow. The majority of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals.

blocks.markdown: **How spillover leads to emerging infection.** (1) A pathogen circulates in a **reservoir host**, often without causing severe disease (bats, rodents, wild birds, primates). (2) **Human contact** with the reservoir or an **intermediate host** (for example livestock or market animals) occurs through hunting and butchering, wildlife trade, farming, or human encroachment on habitats through deforestation and land-use change. (3) The pathogen **crosses the species barrier** if it can bind human receptors and replicate. (4) After spillover the chain may end, or continue as **limited human-to-human spread**, or, if the pathogen adapts to transmit efficiently (effective reproduction number above 1), **sustained transmission** causes an epidemic. Examples: HIV from simian immunodeficiency virus in primates; Ebola virus from wildlife; avian influenza viruses; the coronaviruses causing SARS, MERS and COVID-19. The **One Health** approach links human, animal and environmental health because prevention at the animal-human interface is often more effective than control after human spread.

blocks.caption: Stages from spillover to epidemic
rows: Bushmeat hunting, wet markets, intensive farming, deforestation

blocks.markdown: **The role of surveillance.** Surveillance is the **systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination** of health data so that action can be taken. Its roles in an epidemic: **early detection** of unusual disease or clusters; **confirmation** of cases and organisms by laboratory testing; **describing** the outbreak by time (epidemic curve), place and person; estimating **transmission** (for example doubling time and reproduction number) and severity (case fatality); **guiding control** such as case isolation, **contact tracing**, vaccination, treatment and travel advice; and **monitoring** whether control measures are working. Sources include mandatory **notification** of defined diseases by clinicians and laboratories, **sentinel** sites, **syndromic** surveillance (counting symptoms such as fever with rash before diagnoses are confirmed), **event-based** surveillance (rumours and media reports), and **genomic surveillance** of pathogen sequences. Under the International Health Regulations, countries are obliged to report certain public health events internationally.

blocks.caption: Doubling time t_d of case counts: N_0 cases at the start and N_t cases after time t, assuming exponential growth

blocks.title: Doubling time from surveillance counts
blocks.prompt: Weekly reported cases rise from 50 to 400 over 9 days. Estimate the doubling time.

steps.text: Fold increase = 400 / 50 = 8, which is 2^3, so the count doubled 3 times.

blocks.answer: About 3 days: a rapidly growing outbreak needing urgent control.

items: HIV, TB and malaria dominate global burden, concentrated in low-income regions.
HIV fuels active TB; control needs coordinated prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
Spillover depends on reservoirs, human-animal contact and the pathogen's ability to transmit between humans.
Surveillance enables early detection, description, targeted control and evaluation.

blocks.title: Time is the lever
blocks.text: Faster detection and reporting shorten the period in which an outbreak grows unchecked. Surveillance converts a rumour into an actionable signal.

blocks.title: Treat statistics with care
blocks.text: Global burden figures are model-based estimates that are revised, and reported cases under-count true cases when diagnosis or reporting is weak. Rates need a denominator.

points: HIV, tuberculosis and malaria cause a large burden of illness and death, concentrated in low- and middle-income regions, with HIV driving TB.
Zoonotic spillover occurs when a reservoir pathogen infects humans; epidemic spread requires efficient human-to-human transmission.
Surveillance enables early detection, description by time, place and person, and targeted control such as contact tracing and vaccination.

questions.stem: Which statement about the global burden of malaria is correct?

options.text: Most deaths occur in young children in sub-Saharan Africa
It is evenly distributed across all age groups and regions
It is transmitted by the airborne route
It is caused by a virus

questions.correctOptionText: Most deaths occur in young children in sub-Saharan Africa

distractorRationale.b: The burden is concentrated in particular regions and in young children.
distractorRationale.c: Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes.
distractorRationale.d: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan.

questions.explanation: Malaria burden is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, and young children without acquired immunity account for most deaths. Control focuses on vector control, prompt treatment and prevention.

questions.stem: Why is HIV infection important to global tuberculosis control?

options.text: It greatly increases the risk of latent TB progressing to active disease, so the two epidemics fuel each other
It prevents TB transmission
It makes TB bacilli extracellular only
It protects against TB through CD4 T-cell activation

questions.correctOptionText: It greatly increases the risk of latent TB progressing to active disease, so the two epidemics fuel each other

distractorRationale.b: HIV does not prevent TB transmission.
distractorRationale.c: TB bacilli remain largely intracellular in macrophages.
distractorRationale.d: HIV depletes CD4 T cells, impairing TB containment.

questions.explanation: HIV reduces the CD4 T-cell response that keeps latent TB contained in granulomas. TB is therefore a leading cause of death in people with HIV.

questions.stem: A pig farm worker develops a novel influenza-like virus infection after close contact with a sick herd, but none of her household or colleagues become infected. Which description fits this event?

options.text: A zoonotic spillover that did not lead to sustained human-to-human transmission
A pandemic of a human-adapted virus
A healthcare-associated infection
Antigenic drift

questions.correctOptionText: A zoonotic spillover that did not lead to sustained human-to-human transmission

distractorRationale.c: The infection came from an animal, not healthcare.
distractorRationale.d: Drift refers to gradual mutation in influenza antigens.

questions.explanation: Spillover is the first infection of a human from an animal reservoir. Without efficient human-to-human transmission, the chain ends.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors most increases the chance that spillover will produce a large epidemic?

options.text: Frequent human-animal contact, a pathogen able to bind human receptors and transmit efficiently, and delayed detection
A pathogen that cannot bind human receptors
Early detection with prompt isolation and contact tracing
An isolated population with no travel

questions.correctOptionText: Frequent human-animal contact, a pathogen able to bind human receptors and transmit efficiently, and delayed detection

distractorRationale.b: Such a pathogen cannot infect humans.

questions.explanation: Epidemics need exposure, human infectivity and efficient transmission. Delayed detection gives the outbreak time to grow before control is applied.

questions.stem: Which activity is a core function of infectious disease surveillance?

options.text: Systematic collection and analysis of case data to detect outbreaks early and guide control
Treating individual patients
Developing new antibiotics
Manufacturing vaccines

questions.correctOptionText: Systematic collection and analysis of case data to detect outbreaks early and guide control
questions.explanation: Surveillance turns case reports into information for action. It supports detection, description and evaluation of control measures.

questions.stem: A district of 2.4 million people reports 1 200 new cases of an infection in a year. Calculate the incidence per 100 000 population per year.
questions.explanation: Incidence = 1200 / 2 400 000 x 100 000 = 50 per 100 000 per year. Rates allow comparison between districts of different sizes.

questions.stem: During an outbreak, daily reported cases increase from 30 to 480 over 12 days, assuming exponential growth. Calculate the doubling time in days.
questions.explanation: The fold increase is 480 / 30 = 16 = 2^4, so cases doubled 4 times in 12 days. The doubling time is 12 / 4 = 3 days, a fast epidemic that surveillance should flag urgently.

questions.stem: Describe the global burden of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria, including where it is greatest, and explain how HIV and tuberculosis interact.
markingGuide: HIV: tens of millions living with infection, burden greatest in sub-Saharan Africa
TB: about 10 million new cases a year and over a million deaths, among leading infectious causes of death, concentrated in a few high-burden countries
Malaria: hundreds of millions of cases, over half a million deaths, mostly children under five in sub-Saharan Africa
HIV increases the risk of latent TB becoming active; TB is a leading cause of death in HIV
Control: prevention, diagnosis, treatment, drug resistance concerns
questions.explanation: The three diseases are concentrated in low-income settings and interact through immune compromise and poverty. Numbers are approximate and change yearly.

questions.stem: Explain how zoonotic spillover can lead to an emerging infectious disease epidemic, naming the stages and two factors that increase risk.
markingGuide: Reservoir host (bat, rodent, bird, primate) harbours the pathogen
Exposure through hunting, markets, farming, intermediate hosts
Spillover: pathogen infects humans if it can bind receptors and replicate
Sustained epidemic only if efficient human-to-human transmission (effective R above 1)
Risk factors: deforestation or habitat encroachment, wildlife trade, intensive farming, travel, delayed detection
One Health approach linking human, animal and environment
questions.explanation: Spillover is common but most events are dead ends. Epidemics need transmissibility between humans and delayed detection.

questions.stem: Outline the role of surveillance in controlling an epidemic, giving at least three types of surveillance and three actions that surveillance data can inform.
markingGuide: Definition: systematic ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for action
Types: notifiable disease reporting, laboratory, sentinel, syndromic, event-based, genomic surveillance
Early detection and confirmation of outbreaks
Description by time, place and person and estimates such as doubling time and case fatality
Guides control: isolation, contact tracing, vaccination, treatment, travel advice
Monitors the effect of control measures; international notification under the IHR
questions.explanation: Surveillance provides the information needed to act early and to know whether control measures are working. Without it, outbreaks are detected late.
